title: Tool-Using Agents

content.intro: This lesson covers tool-using agents through 6 syllabus subtopics preserved from the supplied Generative AI curriculum. Treat agentic systems as bounded loops over plans, state, tools, observations, and stopping conditions. Prefer deterministic workflows when they meet the need more reliably.
content.why_it_matters: Web and information retrieval tools concerns how content is represented, selected, or ranked for relevance. Keep the source text and metadata traceable, measure retrieval with labeled queries, and verify that similarity scores correspond to useful results rather than assuming nearby vectors prove factual correctness.

items.title: Database and computation tools
items.text: Database and computation tools describes one part of a controlled action loop. The model may propose a step, but the application should independently validate the arguments, check the caller's permissions, enforce step/time limits, and record the actual tool result before deciding what happens next.

items.title: External service integrations
items.text: Use external service integrations as a lens for understanding tool-using agents. Trace its inputs, the operation or decision it describes, the result a learner can observe, and the limitations that matter for the intended task. Confirm the idea with a small example and an explicit check rather than relying on fluent or plausible output.

items.title: Tool result validation
items.text: Tool result validation describes one part of a controlled action loop. The model may propose a step, but the application should independently validate the arguments, check the caller's permissions, enforce step/time limits, and record the actual tool result before deciding what happens next.

items.title: Permission boundaries and human approval
items.text: Permission boundaries and human approval is a control problem as much as a model-behavior problem. Establish explicit boundaries in trusted application code, minimize data exposure, test realistic misuse and failure cases, and record who is responsible for reviewing residual risk. A prompt alone is not a security boundary.

content.task: Practice web and information retrieval tools within tool-using agents: use a small synthetic input, predict the result, run the example, then change one input to test an edge case. Record the expected result and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example uses a clearly described, non-sensitive input.
Expected behavior and at least one edge/failure case are written down.
The learner checks the result against an explicit criterion and records limitations.
hints: Begin with a tiny input whose expected behavior you can explain before running it.
Change one variable at a time and retain a fixed baseline for comparison.
When a model or external service is involved, inspect evidence and errors; do not treat the model response as a trusted instruction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming fluent or plausible output is necessarily correct.
common_mistakes.fix: Use evidence, schema checks, representative test cases, and human review for consequential results.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing several inputs or parameters at once.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep a baseline and vary one factor at a time so the effect can be interpreted.

common_mistakes.mistake: Putting secrets or private source material in prompts, logs, or a public example.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic data, server-side secret storage, data minimization, and reviewed retention rules.
